articles.title: DTF or silkscreen: which should you choose?
articles.summary: Both methods create great results, but they work differently. Find out how to choose based on your artwork, quantity and the look you're going for.
articles.lead: Both methods can produce great results — here's how to decide which is best for your design, quantity and budget.
articles.imageCaption: DTF is great for detailed, colourful designs. Silkscreen is ideal for bold, simple artwork in larger quantities.
articles.quickAnswer: Choose DTF for colourful designs and smaller runs. Choose silkscreen for simple designs and larger quantities.

sections.heading: How each method works
body: DTF (direct to film) printing transfers your design onto the fabric from a printed film. It reproduces detailed artwork and a wide range of colours, which makes it a flexible option for smaller runs and complex designs.

Silkscreen printing pushes ink through a mesh screen directly onto the garment. Each colour in your design needs its own screen, so it suits simpler artwork — and it gives a durable finish that gets cheaper per piece as the quantity grows.

sections.heading: When DTF makes sense
body: DTF is a good choice when your design has many colours, gradients or fine detail, such as a photograph or an illustration. There are no screens to set up, so a smaller order does not carry a large setup cost.
It is our usual recommendation for caps, t-shirts and polos where the artwork is doing something a screen would struggle with.

sections.heading: When silkscreen makes sense
body: Silkscreen is often the better option for bold designs with a few solid colours, especially in larger quantities. The setup costs more, but the cost per piece falls as the order grows.
It is also known for lasting well: the print stays vibrant through repeated washing, which matters for uniforms and anything worn weekly.

rows: Detailed, colourful designs and smaller runs
Full colour, gradients and fine details
More cost-effective for medium to large runs

articles.closing: Not sure which suits your artwork? Send it over and we will tell you which method we would use, and why.

articles.title: How to prepare artwork for printing
articles.summary: A practical guide to file formats, resolution, colours and common artwork issues (and how to fix them).
articles.lead: Good artwork is most of a good print. Here is what we need from you, and what we can sort out ourselves.
articles.imageCaption: Vector artwork can be scaled to any size without losing its edges.
articles.quickAnswer: Send vector artwork where you can. High-resolution PNG and PDF files may also work, depending on the print method.

sections.heading: The files we prefer
body: Vector artwork — AI, EPS or a vector PDF — is the easiest to work with, because it can be scaled to any size without losing its edges. That matters when the same logo goes on a cap, a tote bag and the back of a jersey.
High-resolution PNG and PDF files may also be suitable depending on the print method. If a vector file does not exist, send the largest version you have and we will tell you whether it will hold up.

sections.heading: Colours
body: Tell us the colours that matter. If your brand has fixed colours, send the references you use; screens and fabric both shift how a colour reads, and we would rather match deliberately than guess.
Designs with many colours or gradients usually suit DTF or sublimation; designs with a few solid colours suit silkscreen or embroidery.

sections.heading: Placement and size
body: Say where the artwork should sit and how large it should be — a chest logo, a full back print, a small sleeve mark. If you are not sure, we can advise on placement as well as on the artwork itself.
We confirm the final placement on the sample before production begins, so there is a point where you can see it and change your mind.

articles.closing: Send us what you have. If the file is not right for the print method, we will say so and suggest the fix.

articles.title: Choosing the right T-shirt fabric
articles.summary: From cotton to performance fabrics, here's how to find the best material for comfort, look and purpose.
articles.lead: The fabric decides how a shirt feels, how it photographs and how long it lasts. Here is how we choose between them.
articles.imageCaption: Cotton, performance and blended fabrics each suit a different kind of day.
articles.quickAnswer: Cotton for everyday comfort, performance fabric for sport and heat, a blend when you want some of both.

sections.heading: Cotton
body: Soft, breathable and familiar. Cotton suits teams, events and everyday wear, and it takes most print methods well.
It is the safe answer when a shirt will be worn casually rather than played in.

sections.heading: Performance fabric
body: Performance fabrics move moisture away from the skin, which is why they suit active groups and outdoor events in Singapore's climate.
They pair naturally with sublimation, where the colour becomes part of the fabric rather than sitting on it.

sections.heading: Blends
body: A blend sits between the two: more comfortable than pure performance fabric, more forgiving than pure cotton, and usually the middle option on price.
If your group will wear the same shirt to a meeting and then to a match, a blend is often the one to pick.

articles.closing: Tell us where the shirts will be worn and we will suggest the fabric — and send a sample before anything is produced.

articles.title: What to consider before ordering in bulk
articles.summary: Key factors like quantity, timelines, storage and sample approval to help you get the best results.
articles.lead: A bulk order is mostly decisions made early. These are the ones worth making carefully.
articles.imageCaption: Quantities, sizes and delivery are easier to settle before production than after it.
articles.quickAnswer: Settle quantity, sizes, artwork and delivery date before production starts — and approve a sample first.

sections.heading: Quantity and minimums
body: Minimum quantities vary by product and customisation method. Ask early, because the minimum can change which method makes sense for your budget.
Larger quantities usually bring the cost per piece down, particularly with silkscreen, where the setup is spread across the order.

sections.heading: Sizes
body: Collect the size breakdown before you order, not after. A size run that is guessed tends to leave a box of unworn extra-larges behind.
We can supply a size chart, or a sample garment to try, before you ask your group to choose.

sections.heading: Samples and timing
body: Most projects take two to four weeks after artwork and sample approval, and complex custom products may take longer. Work backwards from the date you need them.
Approving a sample is the step people are tempted to skip when they are in a hurry. It is also the step that catches the wrong shade of navy.

articles.closing: Send us your date first. We will tell you what is possible before you commit to anything.

articles.title: Merch ideas for teams and events
articles.summary: From staff uniforms to event giveaways, explore popular merch options and how to choose what works for your team or audience.
articles.lead: What to make depends on who receives it and what they will do with it. Here is what tends to work.
articles.imageCaption: The best merchandise is the kind that gets used after the day it was given out.
articles.quickAnswer: Pick things people already use: something to wear, something to carry, something to drink from.

sections.heading: For a team
body: Apparel does the work here — tees, polos or jerseys that make a group recognisable on the day and comfortable enough to wear again afterwards.
Add one practical item people keep: a bottle, a bag or a lanyard with their name on it.

sections.heading: For an event
body: Event essentials — lanyards, badges, stickers, banners — carry the branding, while a giveaway is what the guest takes home.
Choose giveaways that survive the journey home. A notebook or a bottle outlives a printed leaflet.

sections.heading: For a welcome or a thank-you
body: A small set beats a single expensive item: a bag, a bottle and a notebook together feel considered, and each piece is used separately.
Corporate gifts suit the moments where the recipient is not part of the team — clients, partners and speakers.

articles.closing: Tell us who it is for and how many, and we will put together a few options to choose between.

articles.title: How long does custom merch take?
articles.summary: A guide to typical lead times, what can affect delivery, and how to make sure your order arrives when you need it.
articles.lead: The honest answer is that most of the clock runs before production starts. Here is where the time goes.
articles.imageCaption: Most of a timeline is decisions; production is the predictable part.
articles.quickAnswer: Most projects take two to four weeks after artwork and sample approval. Complex custom products may take longer.

sections.heading: Before production
body: The first stretch is the enquiry, the recommendation and the quote. It moves at the speed of the decisions: product, quantity, method and budget.
Then the artwork has to be right, and a sample has to be approved. This is where timelines usually slip, and where they are easiest to protect.

sections.heading: Production and delivery
body: Most projects take two to four weeks after artwork and sample approval. Complex custom products — cut and sew, unusual materials — may take longer.
International delivery can be arranged and is quoted separately, based on destination and order size.

sections.heading: If the date is tight
body: Tell us the date at the start rather than at the end. Knowing it changes what we recommend: a method with no setup, a product already in stock, a simpler print.
There is almost always a version of the idea that fits the deadline. It is easier to find it early.

articles.closing: Send us the date you need them by. We will tell you what is realistic, and what would make it faster.
